parole.testo: Possibly akin to Old Armenian -իչ (-ičʻ), both reconstructible to a tentative Proto-Indo-European *-ikʷyo-s, from Proto-Indo-European * kʷey- (“to gather”), whence also Ancient Greek ποιέω (poiéō, “to do”), Sanskrit चिनोति (cinóti, “to arrange, pile up”).

parole.significato: masculine singular nominative and accusative suffixed definite article: the
parole.testo: Suffixed definite article attached on nouns ending with g, k, h. From the ending Proto-Indo-European *-osyo. cognate to Messapic -aihi. Related to Albanian -i (“of the, etc.”), Albanian i (“of, the, to”).
From Proto-Indo-European *-ikʷyos, which is derived from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey- see Armenian -իչ (-ičʻ)).
Unknown. Maybe a derivation of Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water”).
Unknown. Has been tentatively connected with magar (“donkey”) and derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷreh₂- (“heavy”).

Uncertain. Possibly: # A derivation from Proto-Indo-European *keHl- whence also Proto-Celtic *kaletos (“hard”), Proto-Slavic *kaliti (“to temper, harden”), Latin callum (“hardened skin”). # Borrowed from Germanic, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *jekulaz (“icicle”). # Akin Old Armenian ոյծ (oyc, “col
Uncertain. Hypotheses include: # a variation of soj or lloj. # from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élyos (“other”). # from Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other, different”).

Compound of amë (“mother”) and vis (“land, country, settlement”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“house, settlement”) (compare Ancient Greek οἰκία (oikía, “house (clan)”), Avestan 𐬬𐬌𐬚 (viθ, “royal court”)), literally "mother of the house".

From Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“ancestor”). Cognate to Old High German ano (“grandfather, great-grandfather, forefather”), ana (“grandmother, great-grandmother, ancestress”), Old Prussian ane (“old mother”), Lithuanian anýta (“mother-in-law”).
Enlargement of ang, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰ- (“narrow”). Compare Latin angustus (“narrow”), German Angst (“fear”). Doublet of Latin-borrowed ngushtë.

From Proto-Indo-European *an- (“male or female ancestor”). Compare Old High German ano (“grandfather, great-grandfather, forefather”), ana (“grandmother, great-grandmother, ancestress”), German Ahn (“grandfather, great-grandfather, forefather”) and Old Prussian ane (“old mother”).

parole.significato: so much, so, to a certain degree
parole.testo: Ultimately a formation from Proto-Indo-European *kʷ-. Akin to kaq for which compare Proto-Slavic *jakъ ~ *kakъ.

parole.significato: entertainment (activity designed to give pleasure or relaxation)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ-; argëtoj + -im.
Related to argëtim (“fun, entertainment”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ-.
Possibly a formation from harr (“remove weeds”) or from Proto-Indo-European *arw-, compare German Arve (“Swiss pine”).
From Proto-Indo-European *(ne) h₂óyu kʷíd (“(not) ever, (not) on your life”). compare Ancient Greek οὐ (ou) and Armenian ոչ (očʻ) -ës
Masculine variant of avdosë, compound of *av(ë) (“bird”) + dosë (“sow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis; related to afçë.
From Proto-Indo-European *aṷer, *aṷed (“to make wet”).

Uncertain. Possibly: # From Proto-Indo-European *bʰers- (“tip, point”), whence also Latin far (“emmer, spelt”), Proto-Germanic *baraz (“barley”) and Proto-Slavic *boršьno (“flour”). # Akin to Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon, “drug, medicine”), from a tentative common Proto-Indo-European root *bʰer
From Proto-Indo-European *baba (“barbaric speech”). Compare English baby, Italian bebè (“id”).
From Proto-Indo-European *band (“drop”). Compare Phrygian βεδυ (bedu, “water”), Sanskrit बिन्दु (bindú, “drop”), Middle Irish banna, baina (“drop”) and possibly Latin Fōns Bandusiae.

Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“height”). Cognate to Ancient Greek πύργος (púrgos, “tower”), German Berg (“mountain”). The final velar might have arisen from an earlier singularized plural *birgje (cf. breg ~ brigje), which was later devoiced, although this is speculation.

parole.significato: pledge, oath, word of honor, promise, vow
parole.testo: From be (“oath”) + -së, a formation from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- (“to trust”).
From an earlier *bodse, from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“a type of vessel”). Related to boçe, but took different meaning.

Gheg medio-passive form of boj (“to copulate, to mate”). From Proto-Indo-European *bi-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“in two, twice, doubly”) with -o verbal suffix, ultimately from *dwóh₁ (“two”); compare Ancient Greek δίς (dís, “dis”), Sanskrit द्विस् (dvis).
From bokë, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoHu (“to grow, swell”). Compare Old High German buhil (“hill”).
From an earlier *bodse from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“a type of vessel”).

Uncertain. Compare Sanskrit ब्रध्न (bradhnà, “reddish, yellow”), Proto-Slavic *bro(d)nъ (“colored”), perhaps pointing to Proto-Indo-European *bʰredʰ-n/m- and therefore Proto-Albanian *bradma, though these cognates have had other proposed etymologies.
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰreyH- (“to rub, scratch”).

From Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem- (“to buzz, drone”). Close to Middle High German brummen (“drone, grumble”), Old English brymm (“flood, see”), Latin fremo (“roar, murmur, growl”), Ancient Greek φόρμινξ (phórminx, “zither”).
Latin bulla. Compare Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃-, Middle High German bolle (“bud”), Greek φύλλο (fýllo, “leaf”), Latin folium (“leaf”).

From earlier *burburqe, pluralized form of *burbuk, a formation with root doubling, from Proto-Indo-European *bher- (“to roar, buzz”) (onomatopoeic). Compare Ancient Greek πεμφρηδών (pemphrēdṓn, “kind of wasp”), Sanskrit बम्भर (bambhara, “bee”) and Lithuanian barbė́ti (“clang, clink”).

From Proto-Indo-European *bhrē̆u- (“wellspring”), ultimately from *bʰer-, *bʰrē- (“to bear”). Compare Old High German brunno (“wellspring”), burjan (“to push up, raise”), Old English byrian (“to come up, occur”).

From *bur, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenwh₁, present stem from *bʰrewh₁-, *bʰru-. Compare Middle Irish bréo (“flame”), Sanskrit भुरति (bhurati, “moves quickly, twitches, fidgets”), Old English birnan (“to burn”).

parole.significato: a mythological swamp dwelling monster which takes the form of a steer
parole.testo: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH (“to grow”).

parole.significato: dragoness; mythological creature imagined as a fire-breathing female dragon
parole.testo: A derivative of bush (“monster”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”), originally meaning 'to be wild', structurally similar to bisht.
From bëj (“to do, make”) + zë (“voice, noise”). Alternatively, but unlikely, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).

From an hypocoristic *cullcë, from cull (“child”) + -cë. Alternatively, Jokl derives it as a diminutive of cullak (“naked”) (also related to cull), similar to voc from vogël; Mann relates is to Czech číča (“girl”) and Gothic piwi (“servant”), from Proto-Indo-European *teṷkṷǐə, while Meyer and others

Akin to Slovene cula (“bundle”), Hungarian cula (“bundle”). Barić and Jokl derive it from Proto-Indo-European *k`uts-lo-, akin to Greek σχύτος (schýtos, “skin”), Latin culleus (“leather bag”), and bring the Slovene and Hungarian words derived from it, although the absence of it in other Southern Sla

Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *g(')elt- (“womb”). Compare Sanskrit जर्त (jarta), जर्तु (jártu, “vulva”), Swedish kull (“brood, litter”), Old English child. Çabej links the original meaning to skin, still present is some dialects as cull e mull (literally skin and belly, metaphorically big and sm

Same as the other etymology below, cognate to Armenian սուր (sur, “sword”) and Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌿𐍃 (hairus), from Proto-Indo-European *k'ōros, ultimately from *ḱeh₃- (“to sharpen”). The unified meaning between two etymologies would have been a "sharp cut".Alternatively, a phonetic and semantic variant of
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“to build; house”). Compare Ancient Greek δόμος (dómos, “house”), Latin domus, and English timber.

parole.significato: the first and last three days of March
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes (“three”), with the initial dh- probably deriving from an original compound (cf. dhjetë), from earlier *ndrim, from Proto-Albanian *ən-treima.
Variant of drenjë, from Proto-Indo-European *drew- ~ *derw-, which is possibly from the oblique stem of *dóru (“tree”) or its root source. Occurs in Cham Albanian.
Possibly from the same root as Proto-Indo-European *dóru ~ *dréw- (“tree”), whence dru, drushtë, dry, and droshë, or a derivative from that word.
Either related to Lithuanian drùzgas (“splinter, fragment”), drùžti (“to become weak”) or from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrew (“to crumble, grind”), same root as dromcë.

parole.significato: to throw out, drive away, expel, banish
parole.testo: From dë- + boj, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- (“to run”). Compare Ancient Greek φέβομαι (phébomai, “flee, be afraid”), φόβος (phóbos, “escape, fear”), Lithuanian bėgu (“run, flee”), Latvian bêgu (“flee”), Old Church Slavonic бѣгати (běgati, “flee”).
Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to reel, dissipate, blow; smoke, dark, gray, deep”).

From an older form ênde (attested in F. Bardhi), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“facing opposite, near, in front of, before”). Compare Old Norse eða (“and”), Danish end (“but”), Swedish än (“yet, but”), Icelandic enn (“still, yet”), German und (“and”), English and.

Uncertain. Proposals include: * Inherited from Proto-Indo-European, akin to Ancient Greek σφάλλω (sphállō, “to overthrow”). This appears phonetically incompatible with the current reconstruction of the Greek term's ancestor as Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”). * Borrowed from South Sl
Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pelH- (“to split off, separate”).
Unknown. Maybe from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *plew-, compare Latin pluma.
From Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel-eu-,*s-bhel-eu- (“to split”). Related to flugë.
From Proto-Indo-European *skepska, related to Greek σκεπω (skepo, “to cover, to shield, to screen”).
Either from Proto-Indo-European *sḗh₂l (“salt”), or more likely from gjellë, with a sense development taste of food.

Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu ~ *ǵnéws, relevelled in a preform something like *ǵnu-nó-s. The *ǵ is regularly depalatised before liquids. The shift *gn- → *gl-, aside from a possible parallel in gjuhë according to one hypothesis about its origin, is not seen elsewhere in Albanian, and has

Has been linked to Proto-Indo-European *yemH- (“twin”), although this is problematic both phonologically and semantically. May reflect Proto-Indo-European *sḗmi-ty-om, compare Ancient Greek ἥμισσον n (hḗmisson, “half”), from *sēmi- (“half”). Original *s regularly yields gj before accented vowels. Th
Diminutive in *gogë (“ball”) + -ël (diminutive suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *gag- (“small round object”).
From Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to scratch, dig”). Akin to Old High German grab (“grave”), Old Saxon graf, Proto-Slavic *grobъ (“grave”).

parole.significato: to brawl, to fight, to wrangle over
parole.testo: Either a nasal variant of grij or gërdhij, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrendʰ- (compare English grind, Lithuanian gréndžiu (“to scrape, scratch”). Same sense development as with grih.

A gë- prefixed formation from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smear, stick”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λίπος (lípos, “fat”), Latin lippus (“blear eyed”), Lithuanian limpù (“to stick, glue”), Hittite to smear (/⁠lip⁠/), Old High German biliban (“to stay, remain”).

parole.significato: Austrian pine, European black pine (Pinus nigra)
parole.testo: From the development of the sense “splinter, pointed tip, awn” to “pine needles” (see Etymology 2 below) and then narrowed to the specific tree name. For the semantic development, compare Icelandic barr (“pine needles”) from Proto-Germanic *baraz (“(awn of) barley”). Alternatively from Proto-Indo-Eu
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂erkʷos (“bow, arrow”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₃eros (“elevated”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (Ancient Greek αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn”), Lithuanian aitrùs (“id”)).
Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *sḱéh₃ih₂ ~ sḱyéh₂s (“shadow”), through a late variant *sḱiHeh₂ with laryngeal metathesis.
Variant of hidh (“nettle”), from *h₂idʰ-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (compare Ancient Greek αἴθω (aíthō, “to burn”), Lithuanian aitrùs (“bitter”)).
From Proto-Indo-European *selk- (“to pull”). Compare Latin sulcus (“furrow”), Old English sulh, Ancient Greek ἕλκω (hélkō, “to drag”), ὁλκός (holkós, “draft”). Related to heq.
Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *skew- (“to cover, conceal”).

A formation from humb (“to lose”) + *nerë, singularized plural of *narë, from Proto-Indo-European *nerH-. Cognate with Russian нора́ (norá, “hole”), Serbo-Croatian ponor (“abyss”), Lithuanian nãras (“diving duck; diver”).

Variant of yll (“star”). Related to hyj (“god”). Disputed etymology: *From Proto-Indo-European *h₁us-los (compare Old English ysle (“hot ashes”)), from *h₁ews- (“to burn”) (compare Latin ūrere, Ancient Greek εὕω (heúō, “to singe”)). *From Proto-Indo-European *h₂us-los (compare Sanskrit उ॒स्र (usrá,
Either from Proto-Indo-European *eni (“in”), or a derivative of hinje.
Either a compound of eja + këtu (“come here”), or an isolated imperative form (based on Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”)), cognate to Albanian iki.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰstm̥mos.

From Proto-Indo-European *golbʰ-, *gʷolbʰ- (“conglobate, swell”). Compare Latin globus (“a round body, ball, sphere, globe, heap, clump”), Old Norse kalfabōt (“hip area, hip joint of meat”), Old High German wazzarkalb (“swelling, tumescence through water”).

From Proto-Indo-European *ḱolh₂-m-, enlargment of *kolH- (“awn”) (cf. kalli). Compare Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”), Latin culmus (“haulm”), Old High German halam, Old Prussian salme (“straw”). A loan from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos) or Latin calamus is also possible.
From kalë, or from Proto-Indo-European *keleu (“to wander; way”). Close to Lithuanian keliáuju (“fare, journey”), kẽlias (“way”), Ancient Greek κέλευθος (kéleuthos, “way”).

parole.significato: container or bag (generally for holding food), cone
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)kew-t (“skin, hide”) (compare Welsh cwd (“scrotum”), Latin cutis (“skin”), Lithuanian kutys (“purse, money-belt”), Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “hollow vessel”), σκῦτος (skûtos, “cover, hide”). Related to Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to hide, to cover”). Compare Old En

From Proto-Indo-European *tḱóymos (“village, home”), from Proto-Indo-European *tḱey- (“to settle, cultivate”). Compare Ancient Greek κεῖμαι (keîmai, “to lie down”), (perhaps) κώμη (kṓmē, “burg, unwalled village”), Irish caoimh (“dear”), Lithuanian kaimas (“village”), šeima (“family”), German Heim (“
Probably from the same root of kap, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grasp, take”).

Etymology unclear. The linking particle suggests common development with the names for weekdays, compare e premte (“Friday”). It could be a suffixed form of krye (“head; beginning”) or, according to Topalli, inherited from Proto-Indo-European *kerm- (“to sleep, to rest”); compare Old High German hir

From Proto-Indo-European *grews- (“to crackle, crush”). Compare Old High German krospel, German Kruspel (“gristle”), Gothic kriustan (“gnash”), Lithuanian grukšė́ti (“gnash, rustle, crackle, of sand”).
From Proto-Indo-European *ku̯ak (“croaking, quacking”). Compare Ancient Greek κοάξ (koáx, “frog's croak”), Latin coaxare (“to croak”) and Old Norse kvaka (“chirp, twitter”).

From Proto-Indo-European *gʷei (“to cry, weep”). Compare Old Saxon quīðian (“lament”), Old Norse kvíða (“a trembling, quaking, shaking, terror, anxiety, fear, dread, alarm”), Lithuanian gi̇́edu (“sing, crow”).
From Proto-Indo-European *kuH-l-. Compare Latin cucūllus, Greek κουκούλα (koukoúla, “doll”). Doublet of kukule "silkworm cocoon".

parole.significato: to make (someone) happy; to fulfill a wish; to gratify, please, satisfy
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nóḱe (“he has reached, attained”), perfective of *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”). Cognate with Old Irish tánaic (“he arrived”), Latin nancisci (“to get”), Old English ġenōg (“enough”), German genug, Swedish nog. Alternatively from the compound *ka + *ānda, literally meaning 'havi

A zero-grade, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”) with depalatalization due to Weise's law. Compare Greek καρδιά (kardiá), Welsh craidd, Armenian սիրտ (sirt), Lithuanian širdis, English heart.

From Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to peel, break off”). Compare Dutch loof, German Laub, Irish luibh (“herb”), Latin liber (“bast; book”), Lithuanian lúoba (“bark”). Probably a variant of lapë with voiced labial.

parole.significato: vulgar word, bad behaviour, vulgarity, obscenity, profanity
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smear, stick”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λίπος (lípos, “fat”), Latin lippus (“blear eyed”), Lithuanian limpù (“to stick, glue”), Hittite [Term?] (/⁠lip⁠/, “to smear”), Old High German biliban (“to stay, remain”).
Probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lēg-, *(s)leg- (“to be languid”). Compare Latin langueō (“to faint”).

parole.significato: inhabitant of the historical region of Leknia.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”), a reflection or calque of Ancient Greek Ἀλβανοί (Albanoí, literally “the white ones”), a tribe southern Illyria.

parole.significato: shank, part of the leg below the knee
parole.testo: Singularized plural of *lak, from Proto-Indo-European *(ǝ)lak-, *lēk- (“leg; the main muscle of the arm or leg”), close to Latin lacertus (“limb, arm”), Persian لنگ (leng), Icelandic leggur (“leg, limb”).

An original adjective formation after *lesh, *lesht + *-rik (cf. besnik), reflecting Proto-Indo-European *lak̑is- (“salmon, trout”). Compare German Lachs (“salmon”), Russian лосо́сь (losósʹ, “salmon”), Lithuanian lašišà (“salmon”), and others. The sense development reflects the particular fish color

parole.significato: scale (flake of keratin on an animal)
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *lep (“to peel, flay”).
Probably from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-sko (“to wash”). Orel argues for an early borrowing, from Proto-Slavic *lojь.
Variant of lym, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *lew- (“dirt, mud”). Alternatively, compare Lithuanian lomà, Latvian lãma (“puddle, slop, pit, pothole”), Latin lāma (“puddle, slop, swamp, marsh”).

From Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright, to shine; to see”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “gleaming, white”), Latin lux (“light”), Welsh llug (“radiance”), Lithuanian laũkas (“pale”), Old Norse ljos (“light”).

From Proto-Indo-European *lem- (“open jaws”). Cognate to Lithuanian lemóti (“crave for”), Latvian lamāt (“inveigh, scold, chide”), Ancient Greek λάμος (lámos, “gullet”), Latin lemures (“night ghost, spook”).

Older form of Albanian liqen. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”). Compare Latin lacus (“lake”), Ancient Greek λάκκος (lákkos, “waterhole, tank, pond, pit”), Ancient Greek λεκάνη (lekánē, “basin”), Old English lagu (“lake”). Hyllested and Joseph (2022) argue for a loanword from
From Proto-Indo-European *lep- (“to peel, flay”). Compare Latin liber (“bark”), Greek λεπρός (leprós, “scaly”).
Variant of lëvore, from the root lëv with -ozhgë suffix, from Proto-Indo-European *lep (“to peel, flay”). Compare Latin liber (“bark”), Greek λεπρός (leprós, “scaly”).

From Proto-Indo-European *mn̥tós (“hand”). Cognate to Ancient Greek μάρη (márē, “hand”), Latin manus (“hand”), Gothic manwus (“willing, ready”), Old Norse mund (“hand”). Alternatively, a Romance *manctus based on Latin mancus "maimed, infirm", mirroring the development of Italian manca "left hand".
From Proto-Indo-European *mezg- (“to knit, twist, plait”). Compare Old High German māsca (“mesh”), Old English masc (“net”), English mesh.

parole.significato: to gather, gather in or up
parole.testo: From older mbëledh, from Old Albanian ënbëljedh, made of a prefix ënbë- of disputed origin + a component ljedh from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather”) (compare Latin legere, Ancient Greek λέγω (légō)). For the identity of ënbë-: * Orel reconstructs Proto-Albanian *ambi-ledza, thuse relating the
Possibly inherited from Proto-Indo-European *bʰor-eh₂-teh₂, from the root *bʰer- (“to carry”), prefixed with n-. Compare a possible close parallel Latin forda (“pregnant cow”).

parole.significato: to clasp, enchain, hook, clench, brace
parole.testo: Possibly a compound formation from mbi + thej (“to turn, twist”), a variant of thyej . Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *mer (“to plait, bind; rope”). Compare Old High German bardi (“shield”), Italian barda (“horse harness”), Greek βροχός (vrochós, “cord”).
From mend + -je, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”). Compare Latin mens, mentem (“mind”) Old English ġemynd (“mind”), Old High German gimunt (“mind, memory”).
From Proto-Indo-European *me-.

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mewH- (“fly, midge”), whence also Old Norse mý (reflecting Proto-Indo-European *méwH-ih₂ ~ *muH-yéh₂-s) and more distantly to Ancient Greek μυῖᾰ (muîă), Latin musca and Proto-Slavic *mùxa (all from Proto-Indo-European *mews-). Suffixed with feminine diminutive su
Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *smeḱr-u or a similar variant of original *smóḱwr̥ (“beard; chin”).

From miell, because of its color; from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élbʰos (“white”). Structurally identical with Lithuanian melmuõ (“kidney stone”), Old Saxon melm (“sand, dust”) and Old High German melm (“dust”), both Proto-Germanic forms from *malmaz, *malmōn.

parole.significato: can, to be able to; to have the opportunity, power or ability
parole.testo: Uncertain: Possibly: * From Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”), though there's no evidence supporting the fall of the velar. * A nasal-infixed formation from the root *mewd- (“to rejoice”), whence also mudà (“possibility”), mudúoti (“to try, attempt”) and Sanskrit मुद् (mud, “to be happy, rej

Probably from Proto-Indo-European *men(s)dʰh₁-. Compare Old Norse munda (“aim, strive”), Gothic 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍉𐌽 (mundōn, “look up”), Old High German muntar (“keen, eager”), Ancient Greek μανθάνω (manthánō, “learn”), Lithuanian mañdras (“alert, awake, smart, minxish”).

Uncertain. Probably from Proto-Indo-European *múHs (“mouse; muscle”). Compare Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣká, “testicle, vulva”), Persian مشک (mošk, “lively, eager”), Ancient Greek μύσχον (múskhon, “genitals”), Latin mūsculus (“muscle”), Old Armenian մուկն (mukn, “muscle”).
The initial mën- is either related to muaj (cf. gjithmonë) or Latin mane (“morning”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripern, to mature”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”).
From Proto-Indo-European *nō̆s (“we”).
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥dó (“inside”). Cognate with Ancient Greek ἔνδον (éndon, “within”), Hittite 𒀭𒁕 (/⁠anda⁠/, “in”).
From ndër- + dym, a derivative of dy (“two”), from Proto-Indo-European *du̯is-m̥ (“in two parts”). Akin to Ancient Greek διά (diá, “apart”)

A compound *ne + *-s, from Proto-Indo-European *nō kwe. From Proto-Albanian *(e)nō ̊, from Proto-Indo-European *(h1)nē̆-, *(h1)nō̆- (“after, behind, next to/after”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ἔνη(ς) (énē(s)), ἔνας (énas, “the day after tomorrow”) and Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐍈 (nēƕ, “after”).

From nes (“after”). First attested in the 15th/16th century in Pericope evangelica (from Matthew gospel). Other theories consider the word an adverbial derivative of Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”).

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engʷʰ- (“water-worm”). Compare Ancient Greek ἔγχελυς (énkhelus, “eel”), Latin anguilla (“eel”), Old High German angar (“mealworm, larva, grub”). Occasionally connected to what is believed to be the Illyrian etymon of the demonym of the Enchelei.

parole.significato: to raise, to elevate, to lift
parole.testo: First attested in 1555 by Buzuku as ëngre, allowing the dissection of ën- + *gre. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ger- (“to awaken”).

From gur (“stone”). Alternatively a variant of hungëroj, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to scream”). Compare Lithuanian gùrti (“shrill, shriek, scream”), Sanskrit जरते (járatē, “it rushes, sounds, crackles, shouts”).

parole.significato: protruding part of a bone, e.g. ankle, knuckle, fetlock
parole.testo: From South Slavic; cf. Serbo-Croatian њу̏шка / njȕška (“snout, muzzle, neb”), Bulgarian нюшка (njuška). Alternatively from Albanian noçë, of unclear origin. Possibly from an older *noshë, continuing Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s, *nh₂es (“nose, nostrils”), with the affricatization of the original final

Unclear. Possibly from an older *noshë, continuing Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s, *nh₂es (“nose, nostrils”), with the affricatization of the original final fricative (cf. çaj ~ shaj etc.). Semantically close to Old English nose, nosu (“ness, promontory”), Norwegian nōs (“muzzle, snout”).

From Proto-Indo-European *h₂oren, *h₃eren, *h₃érō. Cognates include Proto-Slavic *orьlъ, and Ancient Greek ὄρνις (órnis). The form orrll has been influenced by the Slavic term. The form orrl is derived from the Slavic term.

parole.significato: mountain nymph; Albanian folk belief pictured as a woman, snake, etc. and whom lived in the mountains, forests, fields,…
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *er-, *or- (“to move, stir, animate, fight, struggle, rise; to spring up, be born”). Cognate to Ancient Greek ὄρνῡμι (órnūmi, “urge on, incite, make to arise, call forth, move, stir oneself”), Latin orior (“to rise; to spring up, be born”), Old Norse iara (“fight”).
From Proto-Albanian *apa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”). Cognate to Messapic [script needed] (apa, “from, out of, by”),[1] Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “away, off”), Sanskrit अप (apa).

parole.significato: a prefix signifying crummy old..., devil of a..., big old...
parole.testo: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w-. Latin paucus (“few, little”), pauper (“poor”), paulus (“small”), parvus (“small”), Old Armenian փոքր (pʻokʻr) and Old English fēaw (English few). However only Ancient Greek φαῦλος (phaûlos) has the exact meaning, suggesting that probably both words have a c

Disputed. Different interpretations have been proposed: # A possible reflection of the sky and thunder god (from Proto-Indo-European *per-en-, an extension of *per(H)- (“to strike”), confer Proto-Indo-European *PeruHnos and *Perkʷunos), attached to *di, the sky-god (*Dyḗws); # Derived from perëndoj

Unknown. Maybe it has the same sense development as Proto-Slavic *pьkъlъ (“hell”), from Proto-Indo-European *pik- (“pitch”), thus cognate to Ancient Greek πίσσα (píssa). If this were the case, it would require Pre-Albanian *pikwa

From an unattested root *pjé + -të, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-, with the meaning going from "in flight" > "in the air" > "above, upwards". First attested in 1555 by Buzuku: "se u ëngriti duoi em e it pjetë përmal, e duojtë taj e kishnë ëngjëruom e prunjishnë për të ënfalë timit." Orel claims i
Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *pelH-ko-s, a formation *pelH- (“gray”) + *-kos. Closely akin to Lithuanian pi̇̀lkas (“grey”), which reflects *pl̥H-ko-s.
From Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁-go. Compare Welsh ôl (“track”), Lithuanian pulkas (“crowd”), Old Church Slavonic плъкъ (plŭkŭ, “army division”), Old English folc (“people, nation, army”).

parole.significato: fully, to full capacity, to the brim
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁tós (“full”), from the root *pleh₁- (“to fill”). Compare Sanskrit प्रात (prātá), Latin com-plētus.
According to Brian D. Joseph, it is a difficult word with unclear root. Hamp claims origin from Proto-Indo-European *pest (“so”)
Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”)

A formation in -shtë > *-est, from posh, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. Compare Hittite [script needed] (pata), Ancient Greek πούς, ποδός (poús, podós), Old English fōt (“foot”). Orel suggests a borrowing from Latin post, poste (“behind, back”), but phonetic problems and a radical change in meaning
Derivative of putë, possibly contaminated with Proto-Indo-European *pṓds (“foot”).

A derivative of përball (“to face, to defy”), from për- + ballë (“forehead”). Structurally and semantically comparable with Proto-Germanic *balþaz (“to be bold”) (cf. Old Norse ballr (“hard, stubborn”)), a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *bʰelH (“white, shining”).
From Proto-Indo-European *peri-seh₂g- (“to drive around”).
From për + pjetë, literally 'for the sky'. From Proto-Indo-European *pro-peth₂-o-. It corresponds accurately to Greek προπετής (propetís, “falling forwards”).
Unknown. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

From Proto-Indo-European *kel (“to drive, force to move quickly”). Cognate to Ancient Greek κέλλω (kéllō, “drive”), Latin celer (“quick, fast, rash, hasty”), Gothic haldan (“drive cattle”), Old High German haltan (“beware, guard, hold, stop”).

parole.significato: to pull out (weapon); to draw out
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *k(')eid- (“to fall, fall upon”). Compare Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), Latin caedō (“fall”), Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”).

Uncertain. Possibilities include: # Akin to Lithuanian šliùrti (“to become dirty”), with the terms sharing a tentative late root Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-r-. # Akin to Lithuanian krèkti (“to coagulate, clot”). # Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كیر (kir, “dirt”).
from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rep- (“to take”)

Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts ~ *h₂n̥h₂tés (“duck”), through an *ih₂-stem variant *h₂néh₂t-ih₂ ~ *h₂n̥h₂t-yéh₂ (eventually *anātyā), an innovation similar to those found in Ancient Greek νῆττα (nêtta) and Sanskrit आति (ātí). The change from n-r can be attributed to rhotacism. Cognates

From rrej, from Proto-Indo-European *ar-. Compare Ancient Greek ἀρνέομαι (arnéomai, “refuses”), ἔξαρνος (éxarnos, “refusing, denying everything”), Old Armenian ուրանամ (uranam, “to deny everything, refuse”).
Possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *Hreǵʰ- (“to flow water”), and cognate with Latin rigō (“to irrigate, moisten”), Proto-Germanic *regną (“rain”).
From Proto-Indo-European *rē.
From Proto-Indo-European *kel (“to stick, sting”).
Orel derives the prefix from the same root as ith (“behind”), namely Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs, through Proto-Albanian *eś-.
A singularized plural of shkarp, a sh- prefixed formation from karp, from Proto-Indo-European *kṛHp-.

From Proto-Indo-European *sel (“to sneak, creep”). Cognate to Middle Irish seilche (“turtle, tortoise, snail”), English slug, Lithuanian selù, selėti (“slink, sneak into”). Perhaps related to the Illyrian tribe of the Seleiitani.
A deverbative formation from shpreh + -je feminine suffix, from Proto-Indo-European *spreg- (“to make a sound, utter, speak”).
sh- (out, ex-) + qit (hit, pull, throw) (qit from Proto-Indo-European *k(')eid- (“to fall, fall upon”)); see Albanian qit (“to hit, throw, pull, etc.”) for more

* Compound of sh- (“de-, dis-, un-”) + dredh (“turn, revolve, twist”). ** Prefix sh- (“de-, dis-, un-”) from the same root as ith (“behind”), namely Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs. ** dredh from Proto-Albanian *drē̆δ-, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreǵʰ-. Cognate to Old Armenian դառնամ (daṙnam, “to turn,

From Proto-Indo-European *(s)treg-, *streg-, *treg- (“stiff, rigid”). Compare German strecken (“to stretch, straighten, elongate”), English stretch. Alternatively from sh- (privative suffix) + ndryqem.
From Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread (out), extend”). Cognate to Latin sternō (“to spread, stretch out”), Ancient Greek στρατός (stratós, “army”), English straw, and others.
From Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to bump, hit”), a formation with the prefix sh- from typ. Cognate to Latin stupeō, Ancient Greek τύπτω (túptō, “to smite”), Sanskrit तोपति (tópati, “to hurt”).

From the same source as gjarpër (“snake”), Proto-Indo-European *serp- (“to creep, crawl”), with ancient epenthesis *sr- > *str- and more recent metathesis *shtrë- > shtër-, or *sr̥- > *str̥- without metathesis.

From Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to spread (out), extend”). Cognate to Latin sternō (“to spread, stretch out”), Ancient Greek στρατός (stratós, “army”), English straw, and others. Variant of standard shtrohë.
Related to Ancient Greek στοιχείο (stoikheío, “element, spirit”). Alternatively from some contraction of Proto-Indo-European *(s)tur- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).
From Proto-Indo-European *tégus (“thick”). Compare Old Irish tiug (“thick”), Welsh tew (“thick”), Swedish tjock (“thick”).

parole.significato: to discolor, to weaken the clothes' colors
parole.testo: From Proto-Indo-European *tragʰ- (“to draw, drag”) or *dʰerǵʰ- (“to bind fast”). Compare Latin trahō (“to pull, carry”), Old High German trehhan (“to push, bump, move, scratch”), English drag.

Pokorny (1959) attributed it to Proto-Indo-European *treb-, *trē̆b, *trōb (“building, dwelling”) (cf. Latin trabs (“balk, beam”), Welsh tref (“dwelling”), Lithuanian trobà (“house, edifice, building”), Old English þorp. Orel and Çabej attributed it to Middle Greek τρέβα "truce", itself from treve (a

Disputed. # From Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós, whence also Latin fūmus (“smoke”), Ancient Greek θῡμός (thūmós, “breath, spirit”), though the voiceless /t/ is unexpected. It may have been influenced by the Greek descendant. # From Proto-Indo-European *h₁éh₁t-mō (“breath, soul”), whence also Sanskrit
From Proto-Albanian *tūpa, probably using the suffix -th, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push, beat”), the same root as shtyp and përtyp.

A compound formation of prefix tër- and heq. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *tragʰ- (“to draw, drag”) or *dʰerǵʰ- (“to bind fast”). Compare Latin trahō (“to pull, carry”), Old High German trehhan (“to push, bump, move, scratch”), English drag.

Possibly from an earlier *tetan, from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people, tribe”). Alternatively from të + tanë (Gheg variant of Tosk tërë (“whole, entire”)). Also a possible doublet of tytë and tul.
Unknown. Probably from Proto-Indo-European *syewH-, with a unique phonetic development.
From Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁ews- (“to burn”). Compare Latin ūrō.

parole.significato: used in questions to emphasise doubt, uncertainty or disbelief.
parole.testo: Cognate with Romanian oare, oară, with the same usage. Likely ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to wish”), though the trajectory is uncertain. Compare German wohl (“possibly”). Used by Buzuku as vollë.
From var, a formation with -g suffix, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“to bind, hang (up)”).

Likely inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₁ter- (“fire”), whence also Proto-Iranian *HáHtr̥š (“fire”) and Latin āter (“black, darkened *(by fire)”), ātrium (“room *(where the fireplace is)”). Also found in Balkan Romance and most Slavic languages, although the presence of va- ~ vo- originating

From Old Tosk *vae, from Old Albanian vōe (still at Malagija), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”). Orel, citing Bopp, Camarda and Çabej, argues the Old Albanian word descends from a borrowing from Latin ōvum. The PIE etymology was earlier supported by Norbert Jokl.
From Proto-Indo-European *wer- + *kʷel-/*wel-.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly akin to Lithuanian vai̇̃sius (“fruit”), alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁ō (“vine”) or perhaps even the same as for the sense “ear”. By some identified as the source of Ancient Greek βαίεσσα (baíessa, “bunch of grapes”).

Probably from an unattested *vetë, *vehtë - to blow (of wind), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Cognate to Serbo-Croatian vetar (“wind”), Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “vapour, steam”), Lithuanian vėtra (“storm”), and others.

parole.significato: a very big person, a giant
parole.testo: A formation from vig, possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to curve, bend; to exchange”). Compare Latin vinco (“to win, beat”), Lithuanian veikiù (“make work”), Old High German wig (“battle, struggle”), wigant (“cripple”), Old English wǣgan (“to torment, smite”). Less likely from viganj
Probably from an older form *vidsa, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”).
From Proto-Indo-European *sweḱrúh₂; compare vjehërr.

Likely a variation of vogë. The meaning "voice" is a secondary formation and an eventual relation to Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs (“speech, voice”) remains doubtful, also due to the very unclear usage of the word.

Uncertain. Attributed to Latin vīvere (“to live”) by Orel, with regular effacement of Latin v /w/ after vowels other than /u/ (cf. latyrë < lavātūra, shqa < sclavus, noshtër < novaster, etc.), although long Latin long i never yields Albanian u in borrowings. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *w

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Either a compound formation of vë + re or from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to observe, pay attention”). Compare (Attic) Ancient Greek ὤρα (ṓra, “care, attention”), Latin vereor (“worship, fear, dread”), Latvian véru (“see, show, notice”), Latin vara (“attentive make, look after; protect,
From Proto-Indo-European *h₁wers- (“to rain”). Cognate with Ancient Greek ἕρση (hérsē), cognate with Latin versare.

From the participle of zbath, from Proto-Indo-European *bhoso-s (“naked”). Cognate to Old Church Slavonic bosъ (bosŭ), Lithuanian bãsas, Latvian bass (“barefoot”), Old High German bar, Old English bær, Old Norse berr (“naked, bare”).

Uncertain. The -b- is most likely epenthetic to avoid the -mr- cluster. Theories that have put forward are: # Akin to Arbëresh zë (“soul”). Compare Romanian inimă (“heart”), from Latin anima (“soul”), which is the only other Indo-European language to have supplanted the original Proto-Indo-European
From Old Albanian zgëledh, zgledh, from zga (“out”) + *ledh (in mbledh), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-. More at mbledh. Also see related zgledh.
From Old Albanian zgëledh, zgledh, from zga (“out”) + *ledh (in mbledh), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-. See related zgjedh.
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

From Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰe or *ǵʰwe. Possibly related to zemër (“heart”), with zemër being analyzed as zem-ërë, meaning "the beating one". The term is exclusively found in Arbëresh and is used in the forms zëe and zëje.
From Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

Treimer and Jokl derive it from a base *skeps, cognate to Latin scobis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”). However, a change from sk- to ç- is unheard of. Çabej considers it a newer word, and groups it with the family of cip, cep, çip, etc., referring to something pointy.
